paras: The lynching of Schenck was the hanging of a one-legged gambler by a mob at Monarch, Colorado, on the night of June 13, 1888, after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon row. The mob hanged him to a telegraph pole, and the dispatch reported that friends of the dead men were gathering and that more trouble was feared. The story reached papers across the country as one short wire item from Salida and was then condensed into weekly news digests.

According to a dispatch dated Salida, Colorado, June 14, a row broke out in a saloon at Monarch the night before. During the row a gambler named Schenck, described as one-legged, was said to have shot and killed George Davis and fatally wounded a man whose name was not known. A mob then "took Schenck out and hanged him to a telegraph pole." The dispatch does not say where he was taken from, whether officers held him, or how many men were in the mob.

The same dispatch closed with the warning that "friends of the two dead men are gathering, and more trouble is feared." No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of further violence appears in the coverage.

The Salida wire ran on June 15 in papers from New York and Portland to Richmond, Sacramento and Salt Lake City, usually word for word. Headline writers cast the dead man as a criminal: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran it as "A Gambler Lynched for Murder," the Salt Lake Herald as "A Murderer Lynched," and the Richmond Dispatch as "Lynched After Killing Two Men." The Silver State printed the same text under "Murder and Lynching. More Trouble Feared," with a Durango dateline and the town given as "Malta." The Omaha Daily Bee was more guarded, heading the item "Hung to a Telegraph Pole" and calling Schenck "an alleged gambler."

News digests reduced the episode to a sentence among storm reports and convention news, the Portland Daily Press stating that Schenck "was promptly lynched." Weekly summaries, such as the Indiana State Sentinel on June 20 and the Kanabec County Times in Minnesota on June 21, carried it a week later. No paper gave the race of anyone involved, and none commented on the lynching beyond its headline.

Copies of the wire differ in small details: the gambler's name appears as Schenck, Schneck and Schenek. The Salt Lake Herald described him as "one-armed" and named the dead man "George Sarrs," readings found in no other copy. The Kanabec County Times dated the row "on the 14th," while the dispatch itself, dated June 14, placed it the night before.

reader.title: Lynching of Schenck (Monarch, Colorado)
bases: Every report says a mob took the gambler Schenck after he shot two men in a saloon row and hanged him to a telegraph pole (A2, A4, A6).

A 'mob' hanged Schenck to a telegraph pole, with no lawful process mentioned, as punishment for killing George Davis and wounding another man; headlines called him 'A Gambler Lynched for Murder' and 'A Murderer Lynched' (A2, A4, A7).

All the reports are copies or condensations of one Salida, Col., wire story of June 14 (A2, A4, A6); no local Colorado paper or follow-up was found, though the core event is not contradicted anywhere.

accounts.label: News-digest condensations
accounts.gist: Weekly and daily digests reduced the story to one sentence: Schenck killed Davis and wounded another man and 'was promptly lynched' or was hanged by a mob.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Salida dispatch nearly verbatim under headlines naming the lynched man as a gambler and murderer: 'A Gambler Lynched for Murder', 'A Murderer Lynched', 'Lynched After Killing Two Men', 'Murder and Lynching. More Trouble Feared.'
News digests gave the lynching one sentence among storms, fires and convention gossip; the Portland Daily Press wrote that Schenck 'was promptly lynched.'

record_check.dossier: The lynching victim is Schenck alone, first name not given; 'Gambier' is the Sun's headline 'Lynched Gambier Schenck', an OCR reading of 'Gambler'. George Davis was the man Schenck was accused of shooting, not a victim of the mob.
No report states the race of Schenck, Davis or the unknown man.
Three deaths reported: Davis shot dead, an unknown man 'fatally wounded' (later 'the two dead men'), and Schenck lynched; only Schenck's was a mob killing.
